lessons.title: Describing village life
lessons.objective: Describe life in the village with clear, connected sentences.
lessons.course:
To describe, we say what we see, hear and do. We use describing words and linking words: first, then, also, in the evening.
Village life: people farm, fetch water from the stream, meet at the market on market day, sit together in the evening and tell stories.

support.title: Useful words
support.text: farm, stream, market day, compound, palm trees, quiet, busy, in the evening

lessons.model: “In my grandfather’s village, people wake up early and go to the farm. In the afternoon, children fetch water from the stream. On market day, the village is busy and noisy.”
lessons.guided: Look at a picture of a village. Say four sentences about it using first, then, also and in the evening.
lessons.exercise: Say one thing people do in the village in the morning.
lessons.answer: For example: they go to the farm.
lessons.remediation: Describe a picture with “I see …” sentences before linking them.
lessons.transfer: Describe your village or your quarter to someone in four sentences.

practice.prompt: Put the sentences in a good order.
items: Early in the morning, people go to the farm.
In the evening, families sit together.

practice.prompt: Which linking word shows that something comes after?
Listen to the description and say what happens on market day.
practice.listen: On market day, the village is busy. Women sell vegetables and men sell goats.
practice.answer: The village is busy; women sell vegetables and men sell goats.
practice.explanation: Listen for the words after “market day”.

lessons.title: Reading a description: the town market
lessons.objective: Read a short description silently and answer questions about it.
lessons.course: A description tells what a place or a person is like. We read it silently, picture it in our mind, then answer questions using words from the text.

support.title: Read silently
support.text: The market of Mbouda is big and colourful. At the entrance, a woman sells ripe pineapples. Further in, tailors sit at their sewing machines. Behind them, butchers cut meat on wooden tables. Everybody talks loudly, and motorbikes hoot outside.

lessons.model: The adult reads the text silently, then says: “I can see the pineapples at the entrance and the tailors further in.”
lessons.guided: Read the text silently. Draw a quick plan of the market: entrance, tailors, butchers.
lessons.exercise: What is sold at the entrance of the market?
lessons.remediation: Read the text aloud with the adult first, sentence by sentence.
lessons.transfer: Describe the market of your town in three sentences.
lessons.materials: The text; paper for the plan.

practice.prompt: Who sits at sewing machines?
practice.explanation: The text says tailors sit at their sewing machines.

practice.prompt: Put the places in the order of the text.
practice.explanation: The text goes from the entrance to the back.

practice.prompt: Find two words in the text that describe the market.
practice.explanation: Describing words tell what the market is like.

lessons.title: Spelling: the apostrophe ’s
lessons.objective: Use the apostrophe ’s to show that something belongs to one person.
lessons.course:
To show that something belongs to a person, we add ’s to the name or the noun: the chief’s palace, Mama’s pot, the teacher’s bag.
We write ’s only for owning, not for plurals: “two goats” has no apostrophe.
lessons.model: The adult writes: “the palace of the chief” → “the chief’s palace”; “the stall of Mrs Ewane” → “Mrs Ewane’s stall”.
lessons.guided: Turn five “of” phrases into ’s phrases. Check that no plural has an apostrophe.
lessons.exercise: Write with ’s: the house of Fon.
lessons.remediation: Use real objects: “This is Bih’s pen.”
lessons.transfer: Write three things that belong to people in your family with ’s.

practice.prompt: Complete with ’s.
practice.explanation: ’s shows that it belongs to one person.

practice.prompt: Which one is correct?
practice.explanation: A simple plural has no apostrophe.

practice.prompt: Write: the bicycle of my brother.

lessons.title: Adjectives: common, proper and comparative
lessons.objective: Use common and proper adjectives and compare things with comparative adjectives.
lessons.course:
Adjectives describe nouns. Common adjectives: big, busy, old, quiet. Proper adjectives come from proper nouns and start with a capital letter: Cameroonian music, English books.
To compare two things we use the comparative: big → bigger, busy → busier, quiet → quieter. Long adjectives use more: more beautiful, more expensive. We add than: The town is busier than the village.
lessons.model: The adult compares two markets: “Douala market is bigger than Bafia market. The village is quieter than the town.”
lessons.guided: Compare pairs of pictures with comparative adjectives and than.
lessons.exercise: Complete: The town is ___ (noisy) than the village.
accept: The town is noisier than the village
lessons.remediation: Practise short adjectives with -er first (tall, small, big).
lessons.transfer: Compare two places you know in three sentences.
lessons.materials: Pairs of pictures (town and village, big and small objects).

practice.prompt: Complete with the comparative.
practice.text: A lorry is [[bigger]] (big) than a car. A city is [[busier]] (busy) than a village.

practice.prompt: Which one is a proper adjective?
practice.explanation: It comes from “Cameroon” and starts with a capital letter.

practice.prompt: Match each adjective with its opposite.
practice.explanation: Opposites help us describe and compare.

lessons.title: Comparing numbers: >, <, ≥ and ≤
lessons.objective: Compare numbers up to 500 with the symbols >, <, =, ≥ and ≤.
lessons.course:
> means “is greater than”: 340 > 290. < means “is less than”: 125 < 152. = means “is equal to”.
≥ means “is greater than or equal to”; ≤ means “is less than or equal to”. If a bus can carry at most 70 people, the number of passengers must be ≤ 70.
lessons.model: The adult compares the populations of two quarters: 425 > 398, because 4 hundreds is more than 3 hundreds.
lessons.guided: Compare pairs of number cards and place the right symbol between them.
lessons.remediation: Compare the hundreds first, then the tens.
lessons.transfer: Compare the prices of two things at the market.

practice.prompt: Which statement is true?
practice.explanation: Same hundreds; 0 tens is less than 5 tens.

practice.prompt: A taxi takes at most 5 passengers. Which numbers of passengers are allowed?
practice.explanation: At most 5 means less than or equal to 5.

practice.prompt: Match each symbol with its meaning.
pairs: is less than or equal to
practice.explanation: The open side faces the bigger number.

lessons.title: Adding numbers up to 500
lessons.objective: Add numbers up to 500 with and without carrying, and solve problems about the town.
lessons.course:
We write the numbers in columns: units under units, tens under tens, hundreds under hundreds. We add the units first. If the total is 10 or more, we carry 1 ten to the tens column.
  246
+ 138
= 384
lessons.model: The adult adds the passengers of two buses: 146 + 138. Units: 6 + 8 = 14, write 4, carry 1. Tens: 4 + 3 + 1 = 8. Hundreds: 1 + 1 = 2. Total: 284.
lessons.guided: Add three pairs of numbers in columns, saying aloud when you carry.
lessons.exercise: A shop sold 235 loaves on Monday and 148 on Tuesday. How many loaves in all?
lessons.transfer: Add the prices of two things you buy at the market.

practice.prompt: When do we carry?
choices: when a column adds up to 10 or more
practice.answer: when a column adds up to 10 or more

lessons.title: Money: shopping up to 1 000 francs
lessons.objective: Recognise coins and notes up to 1 000 francs, pay and give change.
lessons.course:
We use coins of 5, 10, 25, 50, 100 and 500 francs, and notes of 500 and 1 000 francs.
To pay, we add the prices. To find the change, we subtract the bill from the money given: 1 000 − 650 = 350 francs change.
lessons.model: At the market, a bunch of plantains costs 600 frs and tomatoes cost 250 frs. Total: 850 frs. The adult pays 1 000 frs and gets 150 frs change.
lessons.guided: Play market with price labels and play money. Pay, then calculate the change.
lessons.exercise: You buy a book at 450 frs and pay with 500 frs. What is the change?
lessons.remediation: Use prices in hundreds only first.
lessons.transfer: Check the change when you buy something with an adult.

practice.prompt: Total of 350 frs and 425 frs?
Change from 1 000 frs for a bill of 725 frs?
Which coins make 600 frs?

lessons.title: Grid references on a town map
lessons.objective: Locate places on a simple map using grid references.
lessons.course:
A map can be divided into squares. Letters go across (A, B, C…) and numbers go up or down (1, 2, 3…). A grid reference gives the letter first, then the number: B3.
We use grid references to find places quickly.

support.title: Klassia town map (description)
support.text: A 3 × 3 grid. A1: market. B1: church. C1: bus station. A2: school. B2: town hall. C2: hospital. A3: football field. B3: post office. C3: police station.

lessons.model: The adult traces with a finger: “Go across to B, then down to 2: the town hall is in B2.”
lessons.guided: Draw a 3 × 3 grid of your quarter. Put five places in it and give their grid references.
lessons.transfer: Make a grid map of your house and its rooms.

practice.prompt: What is the grid reference of the hospital?
Which place is in A3?
Match each place with its grid reference.
practice.answer: market A1; town hall B2; post office B3.

lessons.title: Living and non-living things in the village
lessons.objective: Compare living and non-living things using the characteristics of living things.
lessons.course:
Living things grow, feed, breathe, move, reproduce, respond to their surroundings and die: people, animals, plants.
Non-living things do not do all of these: stones, water, a house, a car. Some non-living things move (a car) but they do not grow or reproduce.
lessons.model: The adult compares a goat and a bicycle: “The goat eats, grows and has kids. The bicycle moves, but it does not eat or grow.”
lessons.guided: Walk around the compound. List ten things and sort them into living and non-living, giving one reason each time.
lessons.exercise: Is a tree living or non-living?
lessons.remediation: Use the questions: Does it grow? Does it feed? Does it reproduce?
lessons.transfer: Care for one living thing at home (a plant or an animal) for a week.
lessons.materials: A walk in the compound, paper.

practice.prompt: Which one is a living thing?
practice.explanation: A maize plant grows, feeds and reproduces.

practice.prompt: A car moves. Why is it non-living?
choices: It does not grow, feed or reproduce.
practice.answer: It does not grow, feed or reproduce.
practice.explanation: Moving is not enough to be alive.

practice.prompt: Name two characteristics of living things.
practice.answer: For example: they grow and they feed.
practice.explanation: Grow, feed, breathe, move, reproduce, respond, die.

lessons.title: Décrire un lieu : le marché du village
lessons.objective: Décrire un lieu, des objets et des personnes avec des adjectifs, des prépositions et les verbes être et avoir.
lessons.course:
Pour décrire : « Le marché est grand. Il y a beaucoup de monde. La vendeuse a un panier rouge. Les tomates sont sur la table. »
Adjectifs : grand / petit, beau, propre / sale, rouge, vert. Prépositions : sur, sous, devant, derrière, à côté de.

support.title: Mots utiles
support.text:
grand, petit, beau, propre, rouge, vert
sur, sous, devant, derrière, à côté de
être : il est ; avoir : il a

lessons.model: L’adulte décrit une image : « Devant le marché, il y a un taxi jaune. La vendeuse est souriante. Elle a des oranges. »
lessons.guided: Décris une image du marché en quatre phrases avec un adjectif et une préposition dans chaque phrase.
lessons.remediation: Commence par « Il y a… » avec des objets réels.
lessons.transfer: Décris ta chambre en français en trois phrases.

practice.prompt: Complète avec est ou a.
practice.text: Le marché [[est]] grand. Le vendeur [[a]] des mangues.

practice.prompt: Les tomates sont … la table (on).
Relie les contraires.

lessons.title: Many peoples, one country
lessons.objective: Name some ethnic groups of Cameroon and value living together in respect.
lessons.course:
Cameroon has more than two hundred ethnic groups, for example the Bamileke, Tikar, Ngemba, Beti, Bassa, Fulbe, Duala and many others. Each group has its language, its music, its food and its traditions.
Living together means respecting every group, never mocking someone’s language or origin, and learning from one another.
lessons.model: In Manka’s class, there are pupils from many groups. On Culture Day, each one shows a dance, a dish or a song.
lessons.guided: Find out the group of your family. Share one tradition (a dish, a song, a greeting) with the class.
lessons.exercise: How many ethnic groups does Cameroon have, about?
lessons.remediation: Talk about two groups that live in your area.
lessons.transfer: Learn a greeting from a group different from yours.
lessons.materials: A map of Cameroon, pictures of cultural events.

practice.prompt: Which attitude helps us live together?
Match each part of culture with an example.
practice.answer: language: greeting; food: local dish; music: dance.
practice.explanation: Culture includes language, food, music and dance.

practice.prompt: Name one ethnic group of Cameroon.
practice.answer: For example: Bassa, Beti, Fulbe, Tikar, Bamileke.

lessons.title: Rearing poultry and pigs
lessons.objective: Describe how to care for poultry and pigs: housing, feeding, water and cleanliness.
lessons.course:
Livestock farming means rearing animals. Poultry (hens, ducks) need a clean, dry coop, food (maize, bran) and clean water. Pigs need a sty with a dry floor, food and water, and shade.
We clean the houses of animals regularly, we separate sick animals and we wash our hands after touching animals.
lessons.model: Nfor’s uncle shows his poultry: he changes the water every morning and cleans the coop on Saturdays.
lessons.guided: Visit a farm or a compound with animals (with an adult). Write a care plan: food, water, cleaning.
lessons.exercise: What do hens need every day?
lessons.remediation: Start with one animal you know well.
lessons.transfer: Help to feed an animal at home and wash your hands afterwards.
lessons.materials: Pictures of a coop and a sty.

practice.prompt: Match each animal with its house.
practice.answer: hens: coop; pigs: sty; goats: pen.

practice.prompt: What do we do with a sick animal?
practice.explanation: Separation prevents the disease from spreading.

practice.prompt: What do we do after touching animals?

lessons.title: Drawing the plan of our compound
lessons.objective: Say what an architect does and draw a miniature house plan.
lessons.course:
An architect designs buildings. He draws plans before builders start. A plan shows a building seen from above: walls are lines, doors are gaps, rooms have names.
Architects use a ruler, a pencil, an eraser, squared paper and a measuring tape.
lessons.model: The adult draws a plan of a two-room house on squared paper: “This is the parlour, this is the bedroom, here is the door.”
lessons.guided: Draw the plan of your house or compound seen from above. Name each room.
lessons.exercise: What does an architect draw before builders start?
lessons.remediation: Draw the plan of your classroom first: four walls and a door.
lessons.transfer: Show your plan to your family and ask them to find each room.

practice.prompt: Draw the plan of a house with two rooms and a door.
practice.answer: A simple plan seen from above.
practice.explanation: Walls are lines; the door is a gap.

practice.prompt: A plan shows a building seen from…
practice.explanation: A plan is a view from above.

practice.prompt: Match each tool with its use.
practice.answer: ruler: lines; eraser: mistakes; tape: measuring.

lessons.title: Sprinting 30 metres
lessons.objective: Start, run and finish a sprint of 20 to 40 metres with correct posture.
lessons.course: A sprint is a short, fast race. Start: “On your marks, set, go!” Run on the front of the feet, move the arms forward and back, look straight ahead. Run past the finish line before slowing down.
lessons.model: The adult shows the start position and runs 30 m, moving the arms strongly.
lessons.guided: Mark 30 m with stones. Do three sprints with rest between them. A partner times you by counting.
lessons.exercise: What does the starter say before “go”?
lessons.remediation: Run 20 m first, focusing on the arms.
lessons.transfer: Organise a fair sprint race with friends.
lessons.materials: Stones or sticks to mark the track.

practice.prompt: Put the start in order.
practice.explanation: This is the start of a race.

practice.prompt: Where do we look while sprinting?
A track has 40 m. You ran 30 m. How many metres are left?

lessons.title: The palace and the traditional ruler
lessons.objective: Identify elements of culture related to the palace, the traditional ruler and traditional dressing.
lessons.course:
In many communities, the traditional ruler (Fon, Chief, Lamido…) lives in a palace. He has notables and guards. He keeps traditions, settles disputes and leads ceremonies.
Traditional dressing differs from people to people: special cloths, caps, beads. We greet the ruler with respect, following local customs.
lessons.model: An elder describes the palace of the area: the entrance, the meeting place, the traditional dress of the ruler.
lessons.guided: Ask an elder about the traditional ruler of your area. Draw a traditional dress of your people.
lessons.exercise: Name one role of a traditional ruler.
lessons.answer: For example: he settles disputes or leads ceremonies.
lessons.remediation: Look at pictures of a palace and a ruler with an adult.
lessons.transfer: Describe your traditional dress in the family language.

practice.prompt: Match the words.
practice.answer: palace: home of the ruler; notables: helpers; dress: ceremonies.

practice.prompt: Draw a traditional dress of your people.
practice.answer: A drawing of a traditional dress.

practice.prompt: How do we greet a traditional ruler?

lessons.title: Desktop, laptop and tablet
lessons.objective: Distinguish a desktop computer, a laptop and a tablet and say which suits a need.
lessons.course:
A desktop computer has separate parts: monitor, keyboard, mouse, system unit. A laptop has all its parts in one folding case and a battery. A tablet is a flat screen we touch, with the keyboard on the screen. A phone is a very small computer too.
To choose: a laptop for typing on the move, a tablet for reading and photos, a desktop for an office.
lessons.model: The adult shows pictures of the three: “The laptop folds; the tablet has a touch screen.”
lessons.guided: Compare the three devices in a table: parts, weight, battery, use. Advise a teacher which one to buy for typing reports.
lessons.exercise: Which device has a touch screen and no separate keyboard?
lessons.remediation: Compare only laptop and desktop first.
lessons.transfer: Find out which type of computer is used in your school or family.

practice.prompt: Match each device with its feature.
practice.answer: laptop: folds; tablet: touch; desktop: separate parts.

practice.prompt: A trader travels and types a lot. Which device fits best?
practice.explanation: A laptop is portable and has a keyboard.

practice.prompt: Name one device with in-built components.
practice.answer: For example: a laptop or a tablet.
practice.explanation: All parts are in one case.
